value.overview: The Christmas Shearwater is a tropical Pacific seabird that spends most of its life over open ocean and comes ashore mainly to breed. It is a dark, compact shearwater with long wings, a short rounded tail, and a black bill. The species nests on remote islands scattered across the tropical Pacific. Although seldom recorded along the American coast, it has been documented offshore from Costa Rica, where it is considered an accidental or very uncommon visitor.
value.classification: The Christmas Shearwater belongs to the order Procellariiformes and family Procellariidae. Its scientific name is Puffinus nativitatis.
value.identification: This medium-sized shearwater is mostly dark brown to blackish, with slightly paler brown areas on the face, throat, and underparts. It has long, narrow wings, a relatively short rounded tail, dark legs, and a slender black bill with a hooked tip. In flight it shows a dark overall appearance without strong white markings. At sea, its identification can be difficult because it resembles other uniformly dark tropical shearwaters, especially under poor light or at a distance.
value.rangeHabitat: Christmas Shearwaters breed on small, remote tropical and subtropical islands across the central and eastern Pacific, including parts of Hawaii, Micronesia, Polynesia, the Phoenix and Marquesas island groups, the Pitcairn and Tuamotu islands, and islands near Easter Island. At sea they use open tropical waters, often around oceanic islands and productive offshore areas. In Costa Rica, the species is not a regular coastal bird, but accepted records and observations place it offshore in the Pacific, including deep water west of the Nicoya Peninsula.
value.migrationStatus: It is a dispersive seabird rather than a strictly seasonal migrant. After breeding, many birds range widely across the tropical Pacific. In Costa Rica it occurs as a very uncommon, non-breeding visitor or wanderer over deep Pacific waters; records include April observations roughly 35 to 50 km west of the Nicoya Peninsula.
value.breeding: Christmas Shearwaters breed colonially on predator-free or relatively undisturbed islands, often nesting beneath vegetation, among rocks, or in shallow crevices rather than in deep burrows. The female lays one egg, and both adults share incubation and chick-rearing duties. Breeding seasons vary among island groups but commonly extend through much of the warmer part of the year. Nesting colonies are generally remote, and the species returns to land mainly after dark or during periods of reduced activity.
value.dietFeeding: The diet includes small fish, squid, and crustaceans taken at sea. Christmas Shearwaters forage over open water and may feed alone or in association with other seabirds where prey is concentrated. They capture food by seizing items at or near the surface and by making shallow dives or plunge-dives. Their narrow wings and streamlined bodies support efficient flight over long distances while searching for patchy marine prey.
value.behavior: This species is highly pelagic and usually rests on the sea or flies low over the water with measured wingbeats and gliding phases. It is generally encountered singly or in small groups, although several birds may gather where food is abundant. Like many shearwaters, it is most closely associated with land during breeding. Its remote nesting sites and oceanic lifestyle make its population difficult to monitor, and many aspects of its behavior remain poorly documented.

conservation.populationTrend: The overall population trend is not well quantified, but the species remains widely distributed and is not currently considered globally threatened.
